dedupe_keys.name: berlin biotope area factor biotopflachenfaktor for green space in new developments

description: This Climate-ADAPT case study describes Berlin's Biotope Area Factor (BAF), a rule in the Berlin Landscape Programme since 1994 that requires new building developments in the inner city to leave a set proportion of each plot as ecologically effective green space, counting courtyards, green roofs, green walls and permeable surfaces. It was set by experts for different development types after public consultations in 1986 and 1993, to cool the microclimate against an urban heat island of up to 4 degrees, improve soil functions and runoff, and create habitats. Coverage is the inner-city districts of Berlin, Germany, and the rule is binding only where legally binding landscape plans exist, about 16 percent of the city. Costs are absorbed into construction, and owners facing disproportionate costs usually obtain relief; no overall cost evaluation exists. The page is accessible online as free HTML on the Climate-ADAPT portal, published in 2016 and updated in 2026, with links to the Senate's BAF pages and the 2020 review studies. Caveats: benefits for heat and water extremes are expected but not quantified. It illustrates regulation-based green and blue infrastructure for climate adaptation and heat and flood hazard reduction in dense cities; related records are the Copernicus Urban Atlas and the Hamburg Green Roof Strategy case study.
name: Berlin Biotope Area Factor (Biotopflächenfaktor) for green space in new developments
outcomes: Every new development in areas with binding landscape plans must meet BAF targets, which has increased green cover and improved the residential environment and habitat area; climate benefits are not yet quantified.
provider: Climate-ADAPT (European Environment Agency), case study from the GRaBS project and the Berlin Senate Department for the Environment
